decks.title: Database Management System — Part 1: Concepts, Types, Features and Database Design
goals: Distinguish data from information and explain what a database and a DBMS are
Describe the hierarchical, network, relational and object-oriented types of DBMS
State the main features and advantages of a DBMS for accounting
Identify fields, records, data types and primary, composite and foreign keys, and predict when a DBMS will reject a record
Design related tables and explain relationships, forms, reports and indexing

slides.heading: Database Management System
slides.body_md: Part 1 — what a **database** and a **DBMS** are, the **types** and **features**, and how to **design** related tables for an imagined business.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: data and information, database and database management system, types, features, tables and keys, relationships, and design with forms, reports and indexes
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: Every business keeps records of customers, sales and receipts. When those records live in separate files, the same customer is typed again and again, and the files soon disagree. A database management system keeps them together, checks them and answers questions about them. In this part we meet its ideas, its types and features, and the design of related tables, using an imagined wholesaler, Monal Agro Foods of Vidisha.

slides.heading: Data, information, database, DBMS
bullets: **Data**: raw facts as recorded. **Information**: data processed to support a decision.
**Database**: an organised collection of related data. **DBMS**: the software that defines, stores, checks, retrieves and protects it.

nodes.label: Information (dues by customer, sales by city)

visual.alt: Flow from raw data such as invoices and receipts, through the database management system which stores, checks, links and retrieves it, to information such as dues by customer and sales by city
visual.caption: A DBMS turns stored data into information.

slides.narration: Data are raw facts: an invoice number, a date, an amount. Information is data that has been processed into something useful, such as the total each retailer owes. A database is an organised collection of related data, and a database management system is the software that defines it, stores and checks the records, retrieves them on request and controls who may change them.

slides.heading: Tables, fields and records at Monal
bullets: A **table** (relation) holds one kind of thing.
A **field** is a column; a **record** is a row; a blank value is **NULL**.

visual.alt: Monal Agro Foods' Customers table: 5 fields (customer code, name, city, credit limit, agent) and 6 records, one per retailer
visual.caption: Imagined data. 5 fields (columns) × 6 records (rows); NULL = no agent.

slides.narration: Here is Monal's Customers table. Each column is a field, such as the customer code or the credit limit. Each row is a record, one retailer. So this table has five fields and six records. Two retailers deal with Monal directly and have no agent, so that value is left empty, which a database calls null.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: the design behind the table
slides.body_md: Every field is given a **data type** before any record is entered. Monal’s Customers table is designed as shown.

visual.alt: Design of the Customers table: customer code is text and the primary key; name, city and agent are text; credit limit is currency
visual.caption: The design (structure) is fixed first; records are then added through a form.

slides.narration: Before entering records, we design the table. Each field gets a data type: text for codes, names and cities, currency for the credit limit. A customer code is text, not a number, because it is a label, not a quantity. One field, the customer code, is chosen as the primary key, because it is different and filled in for every retailer.

slides.heading: Types of DBMS

rows: Tree; each child has one parent
Fast top-down look-ups; a record with two parents must be repeated
Graph; a record may have several owners (pointers)
A consignment linked to both its customer and its truck
Flexible; complex to design and change
Tables linked by common key fields
Customers, Invoices, Receipts linked by CustCode
Simple, flexible queries; the usual choice for accounting software
Objects holding data and the operations on it
A Product object with its own pricing rules
Suits complex data such as drawings or media

visual.alt: Table of the four types of database management system: hierarchical tree, network graph, relational tables and object-oriented objects, with an example and a strength or weakness of each

slides.narration: Database systems differ in how they link records. A hierarchical system arranges them as a tree, each child under one parent. A network system lets a record have several owners, joined by pointers. A relational system keeps data in tables linked through common key fields, and this is the model most accounting software uses. An object-oriented system stores objects that carry both data and the operations on it.

slides.heading: Features and advantages of a DBMS

rows: A retailer’s name and city are stored once, in Customers; invoices carry only the code
No duplicate or blank invoice number; no invoice for a customer who does not exist
Reports keep working when the storage is moved or reorganised
Several clerks enter invoices and receipts at the same time without clashes
Passwords and user rights: a clerk may enter receipts but not delete customers
Regular copies and a transaction log restore the books after a failure
Questions such as total dues by city are answered in seconds

visual.alt: Table of seven features of a database management system with what each means for Monal Agro Foods: controlled redundancy, integrity rules, data independence, sharing, security, backup and recovery, and a query language with reports
visual.caption: Limitations: cost of software and training, complexity, and dependence on one system that must be protected.

slides.narration: Why use a database management system? Each fact is stored once, so records stay consistent. Integrity rules stop wrong entries at the door. Programs keep working when storage changes. Several clerks can work at once. Passwords and user rights protect the books, backups allow recovery, and a query language turns data into reports in seconds. Against this, it costs money, needs training and must itself be protected.

slides.heading: Keys

rows: Field (or fields) whose value is unique and never blank in every record
CustCode in Customers; InvNo in Invoices
Any field that could serve as the primary key
InvNo; a GST number, if every customer had one
Two or more fields that are unique only together
BoatCode + TripDate in a trips table
Field that refers to the primary key of another table
CustCode in Invoices and in Receipts

visual.alt: Table of keys: the primary key is unique and never blank, a candidate key could be the primary key, a composite key is unique only as a combination, and a foreign key refers to the primary key of another table

slides.narration: A primary key is a field whose value is unique and never blank, so it identifies each record: the customer code in Customers, the invoice number in Invoices. Any field that could do this job is a candidate key. When no single field is unique, two fields together may form a composite key. A foreign key is a field that refers to the primary key of another table, like the customer code inside each invoice.

visual.caption: Primary key (PK) on the one side, foreign key (FK) on the many side.

slides.narration: Tables are related through keys. One customer has many invoices, but each invoice belongs to one customer: a one-to-many relationship. It is built by placing the primary key of the one side, the customer code, inside the table on the many side as a foreign key. One-to-one and many-to-many relationships also occur; a many-to-many relationship needs a third, linking table.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: one customer, many invoices
slides.body_md: How many invoices does each Monal customer have? One count query per customer answers it.

visual.alt: Number of invoices per customer at Monal from count queries: Anupam Annapurti two, Sanchi Provisions two, Saptarshi Traders two, Nirmay Stores one, Gaurang Mart two, Aarohi Foods one; ten in all
visual.caption: Each row: `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Invoices WHERE CustCode = 'C01'` and so on; total 10.

slides.narration: Counting the invoices for each customer code shows the one-to-many link. Four retailers have two invoices each and two have one each, ten in all. Every invoice carries exactly one customer code, so the counts add up to the whole Invoices table.

slides.heading: Designing related tables

visual.alt: Design of the Invoices and Receipts tables: invoice number is a number and the primary key, invoice date a date, customer code text and a foreign key to Customers, amount currency; receipts the same with a text receipt number
visual.caption: Data types: Text, Number, Currency, Date, Yes/No.

slides.narration: To design a business database, list what must be recorded, put each kind of thing in its own table, choose a data type for every field and a primary key for every table, and link the tables with foreign keys. Monal’s Invoices and Receipts tables each carry the customer code, so every sale and every receipt points to one customer.

slides.heading: Forms, queries, reports and indexes

rows: Screen to enter, view and edit one record at a time, with checks and drop-down lists
Invoice entry screen with a list of customer codes
Formatted, grouped output with totals, for printing or sharing
Sales by city with a grand total
Sorted list of a field’s values with pointers to the records

visual.alt: Table of database objects: tables store records, forms are entry screens, queries ask questions, reports present grouped totals and indexes speed up searching

slides.narration: Besides tables, a database uses other objects. A form is the screen for entering and editing one record at a time, with checks and drop-down lists. A query asks a question of the data. A report presents grouped and totalled output for printing. An index is a sorted list of a field’s values with pointers to the records, which speeds up searching.

slides.heading: An index on the customer code

visual.alt: Index on the customer code of the Invoices table: each code in sorted order with the invoice numbers it points to, so the database can find a customer’s invoices without reading the whole table
visual.caption: An index speeds up search and sort; it costs space and must be updated on every new invoice.

slides.narration: Here is an index on the customer code of Monal’s invoices. Each code appears once, in order, pointing to its invoices, so the system can find a retailer’s sales without reading every row. The price is extra storage and a little extra work each time an invoice is saved, so we index only fields that are searched often.

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: data and information, types, features, tables, keys, relationships and database objects

slides.narration: To sum up: a database management system turns stored data into information. Its types are hierarchical, network, relational and object-oriented. It reduces redundancy, enforces integrity and offers security, sharing, backup and queries. A table has fields and records; keys identify records and link tables; relationships are one-to-one, one-to-many or many-to-many; forms, reports and indexes complete the design.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Define a term, then give an **accounting example** (customer, invoice, receipt, asset).
For a primary key, say **unique and never blank**; for a foreign key, say **which table’s primary key** it refers to.
When asked whether a record will be saved, test **three rules**: unique key, matching foreign key, correct data type.
For a relationship, name the type and say **where the key goes**.
A design answer lists **field, data type, key** in a table.
slides.narration: In the examination, define each term and add an accounting example. For keys, say that a primary key is unique and never blank, and name the table a foreign key refers to. To decide whether a record will be saved, test the key, the foreign key and the data type. For a design question, set out each field with its data type and key in a neat table.

`SELECT InvNo, CustCode, Amount FROM Invoices WHERE Amount > 40000;`

Invoice five hundred seven, for forty-one thousand rupees, just qualifies, while invoice five hundred two, for thirty-six thousand, does not. Only the three fields named after select are shown.

sections.heading: 1. Data, information, database and DBMS
sections.body_md:
**Data** are raw facts as recorded: the number, date, customer and amount of an invoice. **Information** is data processed (sorted, filtered, totalled, related) into a form that supports a decision: dues by customer, sales by city.

A **database** is an organised collection of related data stored together. A **database management system (DBMS)** is the software that defines the database, stores and retrieves records, enforces rules on them, lets many users share them and protects them. Accounting software is built on a DBMS: vouchers are stored once and ledgers, trial balance and statements are drawn from them.

**Terms.** A relational database stores data in **tables** (relations); each column is a **field** (attribute) with a **data type**; each row is a **record** (tuple). A field left empty holds **NULL**.

sections.heading: 2. Types of DBMS
sections.body_md:
- **Hierarchical:** records form a **tree**; each child record has exactly **one parent** (region → depot → retailer). Fast top-down access; a record needing two parents must be repeated, and changes to the structure are hard.
- **Network:** records form a **graph** linked by pointers; a record may have **several owners** (a consignment owned by a customer and a truck). Flexible but complex.
- **Relational:** data is kept in **tables** linked by **common key fields** (CustCode in Customers and in Invoices). Simple to understand, flexible queries in SQL; the model used by most accounting software.
- **Object-oriented:** data is stored as **objects** that carry both their data and the operations on it; suits complex data such as designs and media.

sections.heading: 3. Features and advantages (and limitations)
sections.body_md:
**Features and advantages:**
1. **Controlled redundancy** and **consistency**: each fact stored once.
2. **Integrity**: rules on keys, data types and links stop wrong entries.
3. **Data independence**: programs do not change when storage changes.
4. **Sharing and concurrency control**: many users at once, with record locking.
5. **Security**: passwords, user rights, audit trail.
6. **Backup and recovery** from a failure using backups and a transaction log.
7. **Query language and reports**: information on demand.

**Limitations:** cost of software, hardware and training; complexity; dependence on one system, which must itself be secured and backed up.

Passwords and user rights: a clerk may enter receipts but not delete customers

sections.heading: 4. Tables, data types and keys
sections.body_md:
**Designing a table:** name it after the thing it records; list its fields; give each a **data type** (text, number, currency, date, Yes/No); choose a **primary key**.

**Keys:**
- **Primary key**: a field whose value is **unique and never blank** in every record (CustCode, InvNo, AssetNo).
- **Candidate key**: any field that could be the primary key.
- **Composite key**: two or more fields unique only together (BoatCode + TripDate).
- **Foreign key**: a field that refers to the **primary key of another table** (CustCode in Invoices). It may repeat but must match an existing record.

**Integrity rules the DBMS enforces** (see the table): it refuses a duplicate or blank primary key, a foreign key with no matching parent, a value of the wrong type, and the deletion of a parent record still referred to.

sections.body_md:
**Relationships:** **one-to-one** (an employee and one salary account), **one-to-many** (a customer and its invoices: the primary key of the one side goes into the many side as a foreign key), **many-to-many** (invoices and products: a linking table holds both keys).

**Database objects:**
- **Form**: screen for entering, viewing and editing one record at a time, with checks and drop-down lists.
- **Query**: a question asked of the data (in SQL).
- **Report**: formatted output of many records, grouped and sorted with subtotals and totals, for printing; may combine related tables (sales by city: invoices linked to customers).
- **Index**: a sorted list of a field’s values with pointers to records; speeds up searching and sorting, costs space and slows saving a little.

sections.heading: 6. SQL basics: SELECT, WHERE, AND, OR, UPDATE, DELETE
sections.body_md:
- `SELECT field1, field2 FROM table WHERE condition;` shows the chosen fields of the records that meet the condition; `SELECT *` shows all fields. SELECT never changes data.
- **AND**: both conditions true (narrows). **OR**: at least one true (widens). **AND is applied before OR**; use brackets to change the order.
- `UPDATE table SET field = value WHERE condition;` changes values; the new value may use the old one (`CreditLimit = CreditLimit + 20000`).
- `DELETE FROM table WHERE condition;` removes records; the table design remains.
- Without WHERE, UPDATE and DELETE act on **every** record. Run the same WHERE with SELECT first.

Text and dates are written in single quotes (`'Vidisha'`, `'2026-04-15'`); numbers are not. Dates written year-month-day compare correctly.

sections.heading: 7. Aggregate functions: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MAX, MIN
sections.body_md:
Aggregate functions return **one value** from many records: `COUNT(*)` (number of records), `COUNT(field)` (records with a value in that field), `SUM(field)`, `AVG(field)`, `MAX(field)`, `MIN(field)`.

- WHERE is applied **first**, then the function: `SELECT SUM(Amount) FROM Invoices WHERE CustCode = 'C05';` gives the sales to one customer.
- **NULLs are skipped** by every function except COUNT(*); AVG divides by the number of values present.
- Several functions may be used together: `SELECT MAX(Balance), MIN(Balance) FROM Debtors;`.

Accounting uses: total sales or dues, number of invoices, average invoice, highest balance, smallest receipt.

sections.heading: 8. DBMS in business: debtors and creditors, bank reconciliation, asset accounting
sections.body_md:
**Accounting information.** Each source document is entered once (through a form) into linked tables; ledgers, the trial balance, statements and management reports are drawn from them, so they always agree.

**Debtors and creditors.** Customers and Suppliers are master tables; invoices, bills, receipts and payments carry the party code as a foreign key. A report gives each balance (opening + invoices − receipts), dues past their date, and parties over their credit limit.

**Bank reconciliation.** The bank statement is imported as a table and matched with the bank column of the cash book on the reference. Unmatched items are the reconciling items: cheques issued but not presented and bank-only credits are added to the cash book balance; cheques deposited but not credited and bank-only debits are subtracted, giving the pass book balance.

**Asset accounting.** A fixed asset register table holds each asset’s number, category, date, cost, rate and location; the DBMS computes depreciation and written-down values and totals them by category.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Calling a code field "number" because it holds digits: codes are **text**.
- Saying a foreign key must be unique (only the **primary** key must be).
- Forgetting that a primary key can never be **blank**.
- Mixing AND and OR without brackets, or forgetting that **AND comes first**.
- Writing text or dates **without quotes**, or numbers with them.
- Using UPDATE or DELETE **without WHERE**.
- Counting a NULL in COUNT(field) or dividing AVG by all the rows when some are NULL.
- In a bank reconciliation, adding a deposit not yet credited instead of subtracting it.

**How marks are usually split**
- 1 mark: a term, a key, a function, or the result of one simple query.
- 2 marks: a distinction (data and information, form and report), or one query with its result.
- 3 marks: three features or types, three key verdicts, or the outputs of three queries.
- 5 marks: a design (fields, types, keys and relationship), or queries with outputs, or a debtors report or bank reconciliation from tables.

questions.stem_md: The accounts office of Tragopan Tea Traders Ltd, an imagined company in Namchi, keeps its customer, invoice and receipt records together in one database. The software that creates this database, stores and retrieves its records and controls who may change them is called
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** a database management system (DBMS). A DBMS is the software layer between the users and the stored records: it defines the tables, stores and retrieves records, enforces the rules on them and controls access.

questions.stem_md: Hoopoe Spices Ltd, an imagined wholesaler in Etawah, records every credit sale in its database. Which of the following is **information** rather than raw data for its credit controller?

options.text_md: The amount keyed in for one sales invoice
The date typed on one receipt
The code given to one retailer in the customer table
A report of the total amount each retailer owes at the month end, highest first

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** A report of the total amount each retailer owes at the month end, highest first. Data are raw facts as recorded (one amount, one date, one code). Information is data processed into a form that helps a decision: here, invoices less receipts, totalled per retailer and sorted.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** hierarchical model. A tree in which every child record has exactly one parent (region → depot → retailer) is the hierarchical model. Reaching a retailer means going down the tree from its region.

relational model, in which tables are linked only through key values
network model, in which a record may have more than one owner record
flat-file model, in which everything sits in one list

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** network model, in which a record may have more than one owner record. A consignment owned by two parents (a customer and a truck) through pointers is the network (graph) model; a hierarchy allows only one parent, and a relational database links tables through key values rather than pointers.

After moving to a DBMS it keeps the address once, in a Dealers table, and every other table refers to it by dealer code. Which advantage of a DBMS does this show?

Controlled redundancy, which also keeps the address consistent everywhere
Security through passwords and user rights

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Controlled redundancy, which also keeps the address consistent everywhere. Storing a fact once and referring to it by key removes duplicate copies, so an address change is made in one place and every report shows the same address.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** concurrency control (multi-user access with locking). A DBMS lets many users work on shared records at once and locks a record while it is being changed, so simultaneous updates do not clash.

questions.solution_md: **True.** Backup and recovery is a standard DBMS feature: the last backup is restored and the logged transactions after it are re-applied.

questions.stem_md: Trogon Cement Agencies, an imagined dealer in Satna, is moving its debtors records into a DBMS. Name and explain two features of a DBMS that will help its accountant keep these records correct and safe.
questions.solution_md: One mark for each feature that is both named and linked to correctness or safety of the debtors records.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Integrity (validation) rules.** The DBMS checks every entry against rules set once: a primary key such as the customer code must be unique and filled in, an amount must be a number, and an invoice must quote a customer code that exists. Wrong or incomplete records are refused at the point of entry.
2. **Security and backup.** Each user logs in with a password and gets only the rights needed (a clerk may enter receipts but not delete customers), and the DBMS keeps backups and a transaction log so records can be restored after a failure.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between data and information, using the sales records of Prinia Bakery Supplies Ltd, an imagined company in Raigarh, as your example.
questions.solution_md: Define both terms and give one Prinia example of each.

answer.model_answer_md:
- **Data** are raw, unprocessed facts as they are recorded, for example the invoice number, date, customer code and amount of each sale Prinia keys into its Invoices table. Taken one by one they do not answer a business question.
- **Information** is data that has been processed (sorted, filtered, totalled, related) into a meaningful form that supports a decision, for example a report of total sales by customer for June, or the list of customers whose dues exceed their credit limit.

A DBMS turns the stored data into information through queries and reports.

marking_scheme.step: Data defined as raw facts, with an example
Information defined as processed, meaningful data, with an example

questions.stem_md: Pipit Stationers Ltd, an imagined company in Azamgarh, keeps three separate spreadsheet files: one for sales, one for receipts and one for customer addresses. The same customer is often spelt differently in each file. Give three advantages Pipit would gain by moving these records into a single relational database.
questions.solution_md: Tie each advantage to the problem of three unlinked files with differently spelt customers.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Less redundancy, more consistency.** Each customer’s name and address are stored once in a Customers table; sales and receipts refer to the customer code, so one spelling appears in every report and a change is made in one place.
2. **Integrity rules.** The DBMS refuses a sale or receipt for a customer code that does not exist, a duplicate invoice number or an amount typed as text, so errors are stopped at entry.
3. **Queries and reports on related data.** Because the tables are linked by keys, Pipit can ask for the balance of every customer (sales less receipts) or the dues by town in seconds, without copying figures between files.

*(Also accepted: shared multi-user access, security through user rights, backup and recovery.)*

marking_scheme.step: Reduced redundancy and consistent customer records
Queries and reports across linked tables (or another valid advantage)

questions.stem_md: Wagtail Cold Stores Ltd, an imagined company in Bilaspur, stores apples for many growers in several chambers. Explain the hierarchical, network and relational types of DBMS, showing how each could hold its grower and storage records.
questions.solution_md: For each type: its structure, one Wagtail example, and one strength or weakness.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Hierarchical.** Records form a tree: each child has one parent. Wagtail could keep chamber → rack → lot, with every lot under one rack. Simple and fast for top-down look-ups, but a lot that must also be linked to its grower cannot have a second parent, so data gets repeated.
2. **Network.** Records form a graph linked by pointers, and a record may have several owners. A lot can be owned both by its chamber and by its grower. More flexible, but the pointer structure is complex to design and change.
3. **Relational.** Data is kept in tables (Growers, Chambers, Lots) linked through key fields: each Lots row carries the GrowerCode and ChamberCode as foreign keys. Any question (lots of one grower, space used in a chamber) can be answered by a query; this is the model most accounting software uses.

marking_scheme.step: Relational: linked tables with keys, example

questions.stem_md: Fantail Fans Ltd, an imagined company, looks up its customer ledger of thousands of records by customer code many times a day. Explain what indexing a field means, with one advantage and one drawback for Fantail.
questions.solution_md: Meaning with the book-index idea, then one gain and one cost.

answer.model_answer_md:
- **Meaning.** An index on a field (say CustCode) is a separate, sorted list of that field’s values, each with a pointer to the record holding it, so the DBMS can jump to the right records instead of reading the whole table, just as a book’s index points to pages.
- **Advantage:** searches, sorts and links on CustCode become much faster as the ledger grows.
- **Drawback:** the index takes extra storage and must be updated whenever a record is added, changed or deleted, which slows data entry slightly.

questions.stem_md:
Bunting Builders Ltd, an imagined construction company, wants to keep its fixed asset register in a database. For each asset it records an asset number, the name of the asset, its category (plant and machinery, vehicles, or furniture and fittings), the date of purchase, the cost and whether it is still in use. The depreciation rate depends only on the category.

(a) Design an Assets table: list its fields with a suitable data type for each, and choose its primary key with a reason. (3)

(b) Explain why the depreciation rate should be kept in a separate Categories table, design that table, and state the key that links the two tables and the type of relationship. (2)
questions.solution_md: Choose types by what each field holds (codes are text, money is currency, dates are dates, in-use is Yes/No); move the category-dependent rate to its own table and link it by key.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a) Assets table**

| Field | Data type | Key |
| --- | --- | --- |
| AssetNo | Text | Primary key |
| AssetName | Text |   |
| CatCode | Text | Foreign key → Categories |
| PurchaseDate | Date |   |
| Cost | Currency |   |
| InUse | Yes/No |   |

AssetNo is the primary key: every asset gets its own number, never blank; names (two "Concrete mixer"s are possible), dates, categories and costs can repeat. Example records: A-01 Concrete mixer, PM, 2025-04-01, 380000, Yes; A-02 Tipper truck, VH, 2024-04-01, 1450000, Yes.

**(b) Categories table**

| Field | Data type | Key |
| --- | --- | --- |
| CatCode | Text | Primary key |
| CatName | Text |   |
| RatePct | Number |   |

Keeping the rate in Assets would repeat it in every asset of a category, and a rate change would have to be made in many rows (risking inconsistency). In Categories it is stored once. CatCode, the primary key of Categories, appears in Assets as a **foreign key**; one category has many assets, so the relationship is **one-to-many**. The DBMS will then refuse an asset with category XX ("no matching record in Categories") or a second asset numbered A-02 ("duplicate primary key").

marking_scheme.step: Six fields with suitable data types
Categories table, foreign key CatCode, one-to-many

questions.stem_md: Pochard Pumps Ltd, an imagined company, plans to run its accounts on a database. Explain how a DBMS would support (i) its debtors and creditors records, (ii) its bank reconciliation and (iii) its fixed asset accounting.
questions.solution_md: For each area: what is stored, how it is linked, and what the DBMS produces from it.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Debtors and creditors.** Customers and suppliers are master tables; each invoice, bill, receipt and payment is stored once with the party’s code as a foreign key. Queries give any party’s balance, the list of dues past their date and parties over their credit limit, and the DBMS refuses a bill for a party not on file.
2. **Bank reconciliation.** The bank column of the cash book and the bank statement (imported as a table) are matched on the cheque or transaction reference. Unmatched items, such as cheques not yet presented or credited, bank charges and interest, are listed automatically to prepare the reconciliation statement.
3. **Asset accounting.** A fixed asset register table holds each asset’s number, category, date, cost, rate and location. Depreciation and written-down values are computed for every asset, totals by category feed the accounts, and disposals are traced by asset number.
